concepts.note: where DLS decides 4 games per season

faq.q: What does DLS do?
faq.a: Resets target by overs x wickets resource — 50 overs 10 wickets 100% vs 30 overs 59%, not just run-rate's overs linear.

faq.q: What is minimum overs for DLS?
faq.a: 20 in ODI, 5 in T20 — no result if rain before 20 in ODI, not DLS at 18.

faq.q: Why DLS not run-rate?
faq.a: Wickets matter — 100-2 in 20 needs 222 not 178, because 100-2 resource is 74% vs 59% for 0-0 in 30, so wickets shift par 44 runs.

explainers.question: What is the powerplay in cricket?
explainers.short: Powerplay, explained
explainers.answer: The powerplay is the fielding restriction of overs 1-10 with 2 fielders outside the 30-yard circle, overs 11-40 with 4 outside, overs 41-50 with 5 outside — the 10-30-10 split in ODI that decides 320 par, not the batting team's choice, with T20's 6 overs powerplay 2 outside then 14 with 5.
explain: The ODI powerplay is 10-30-10. Overs 1-10 2 fielders outside circle, 11-40 4 outside, 41-50 5 outside, plus 2 fielders in catching positions in 1-10 — the 10 with 2 outside forces the openers to hit over the top for 4s inside, which is why the powerplay 1-10 goes at 60 per 10 vs middle 40-45 per 10, but middle's 30 with 4 outside is the build, not slog — the 10-30-10 decides the 50's shape: powerplay 60, middle 135, death 125 =320 par.

The T20 powerplay is 6 overs with 2 outside, 14 with 5 outside. The T20 20 overs split 6 with 2 outside then 14 with 5 — the 6 is 50-55 vs 170 par, so the powerplay is 30% of innings, not 20% as ODI's 10 is 20% — the 6 with 2 makes the T20 opeler's 30 off 18 more valuable than ODI's 30 off 30, which is why the IPL's 6-over 55 sets the 170, not the ODI's 10-over 60, and why the 6's 2-outside is the 10's twin with 20% less time.

The batting choice powerplay is old ODI before 2015 — the batting powerplay 5 overs with 3 outside was chosen by batting side overs 11-40, removed 2015 to fix the 10-30-10 mandatory, which is why the 2023 World Cup's powerplay's 10-30-10 is not chosen — the 2011 World Cup had batting and bowling powerplays, the 2015 law replaced with 10-30-10 default.

The field circle matters. The 30-yard circle is 30 yards from stumps, within which 4 fielders must be in powerplay 1, 2 catchers in that 4 — the 4 inside the circle is the bottleneck that 2 outside leaves 7 inside including keeper and bowler, so the 2-outside powerplay is 7 inside, not 9 as 5 outside later, which is why the powerplay's 2 allows the loopy 4 over mid-off, not the flat 6 over extra cover vs 5 outside.

The evergreen myth is powerplay is batting choice. Since 2015 it is fixed 10-30-10 — the captain not the batter decides no choice, which is why the powerplay's 10-30-10 shape is 60 + 135 +125 =320, not the batter's 5-over choice, and why T20's 6 plus 5-outside 14 is also fixed, not optional, like football's 15-min halftime fixed, not the captain's.
explainers.example: World Cup 2023 powerplay: Rohit Sharma 40 off 24 in first 10 with 2 outside vs Australia, middle 11-40 with 4 outside 135, death 41-50 with 5 outside 125 — 10-30-10 =320 par, T20's 6 with 2 then 14 with 5 =50 in 6 — the 10 with 2 to 30 with 4 to 10 with 5 that 2015 made mandatory, not batting choice, 30-yard circle 7 inside not 9.

myths.belief: Powerplay is batter's choice.
myths.reality: Fixed 10-30-10 ODI — 1-10 2 outside, 11-40 4 outside, 41-50 5 outside — not chosen since 2015, and T20's 6 plus 14 is also fixed.

myths.belief: Powerplay is 20% of innings.
myths.reality: 10 of 50 =20% ODI, but 6 of 20 =30% T20 — so T20 powerplay 55 in 6 sets 170, ODI's 60 in 10 plus middle 135 death 125 sets 320.

myths.belief: Field is open in powerplay.
myths.reality: Powerplay 1-10 only 2 outside means 7 inside — 4 in the 30-yard circle with 2 catchers — not the 5-outside's 6 inside later.

concepts.label: DLS
concepts.note: why 10 with 2 sets resource, not just 50

faq.q: What is powerplay in ODI?
faq.a: 1-10 2 fielders outside 30-yard circle, 11-40 4 outside, 41-50 5 outside — 10-30-10, not batter choice since 2015.

faq.q: What is T20 powerplay?
faq.a: 1-6 2 outside, 7-20 5 outside — 6 overs of 20, 30% of innings, not 20% as ODI's 10.

faq.q: Why does powerplay decide par?
faq.a: Powerplay 60 per 10 plus middle 135 plus death 125 =320 par — the shape, not just the total, sets the 50-over chase.

explainers.question: What is the Cricket World Cup?
explainers.short: Cricket World Cup, explained
explainers.answer: The ODI Cricket World Cup is 10 teams over 47 days every 4 years — 10 play a single round-robin 9 games each, top 4 to semis, single elimination to the final over 100 overs per day, not 20, with the 2023 India 10-0 group then 12-man heartbreak the evergreen.
explain: The ODI World Cup is 10 teams in 2023 and 2027 — 10 play single round-robin 9 each over 45 days, then 1st vs 4th and 2nd vs 3rd semis single game over 100 overs (50 per side), final over 100 overs at Ahmedabad's 132,000 — the 10 not 32 makes the 9-group the league, not the group, which is why Afghanistan's 4 wins in 2023 still meant 6th and out, while 4 in football's 3-group can mean knockout — the 9 vs 3 defines the footprint.

The qualifier explains India 2023's depth. The World Cup Qualifier with 10 teams for the last 2 spots — 2 of 32 Associates plus Full Members — Sri Lanka and Netherlands qualified via Zimbabwe 2023 for the 10, so the 10 are 8 auto plus 2 via qualifier, which is why West Indies missed the 2023 World Cup for the first time — the 10, not 14 as in 2015, needs 2 via qualifier, not just ranking, so the 2015 14-team left no qualifier bottleneck but the 10-team did.

The 50 overs explains the day. One innings 50 overs of 6 balls — 300 balls per innings, 600 per day, 8 hours including lunch, with powerplay 10 overs with 2 fielders outside circle, 30 overs with 4 outside, 10 with 5 outside — the powerplay's 10-30-10 sets the field that decides 320 par, not the 200 of T20's 20 overs, which is why the ODI 400 is rare and 320 is par, not 170 as in T20 or 450 as in Test's 90 overs per day.

The evergreen is 2019 tie. England vs New Zealand tie 241-241 in the final, super over tie 15-15, boundary countback gave England the win on 26-17 — the law since changed to successive super overs until win, no countback — the 2019 26-17 boundary is the only World Cup won on boundaries, not runs, which is why the ODI laws now have two super overs, not one plus boundaries, like football's away goals now removed.

The T20 World Cup is 20 teams now 2024 — 20 teams, 4 groups of 5, top 2 to Super 8, then semis — the ODI is 10 over 47 days, T20 20 over 29 days, so the ODI's single round-robin 9 is the endurance league, T20's 5-group is the sprint, which is why the IPL's 74 games feed the T20 World Cup more than the ODI — the 50 vs 20 splits the preparation.

explainers.question: What is the T20 World Cup?
explainers.short: T20 World Cup, explained
explainers.answer: The T20 World Cup is 20 teams every 2 years over 28 days — 20 play 4 groups of 5, top 2 to Super 8, top 4 to semis, single 20-over 3-hour games, winner plays 9 games not 50 overs, with the 2026 India defence the 20-team 9-game path that the ODIs 10-team 9-game mirrors in time not overs.
explain: The T20 World Cup is 20 since 2024 expanded from 16 — 4 groups of 5 over 12 days, top 2 per group to Super 8, Super 8 as 2 groups of 4, top 2 per to semis single knockout — the 20's 4x5 means 4 group games per team, not 9 as ODI's 10 single round-robin, which is why Uganda and USA made 2024 as the 20's Associates 8 of 20, while ODI's 10 has 0 Associates via qualifier except Netherlands — the 20 gives 8 Associate spots, the 10 gives 2.

The Super 8 explains the stage. After 4x5, the 8 carry over seeding not points — 8 to 2 groups of 4 play 3 each, top 2 to semis — the Super 8 is 3 games not 4, so the 2024 Super 8 Group 1 had India, Australia, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, each 3 — the 8's 3 decides the semi with one surprise (Afghanistan over Australia), which is why the T20 World Cup's Super 8 is the ODI's top 4 semis' twin with 8 not 4, longer but still single KO after.

The 20-over shapes the 3 hours. Twenty overs per side, 120 balls per innings, 6 overs powerplay 2 outside then 14 with 5, innings 90 minutes plus 20 interval, game 3:30, not ODI's 8 hours or Test's 30 hours — the T20's 120 balls par 170 means 8 per over vs ODI's 320 at 6.4 per over, which is why the T20's 6 vs 14 powerplay's 55 in 6 is 30% of innings, not 20% as ODI's 10, and why IPL's 74 games in 20 overs feeds the T20 World Cup's 20-over, not 50.

The evergreen is 2024 co-host. USA and West Indies co-host 2024 with USA beating Pakistan in group, which is why the 20's co-host's 2 games at 6am India prime-time matter as the 20's gate for Associates — the associate 8 of 20 got Dallas's 6am game because India's prime was Dallas midnight, which is why the 20's Dallas 2024 surface issue was the 6am start for India, not for Dallas, like AFCON's 14:00 for Europe vs 17:00 for Africa.

The qualifier feeds the 20. The 20 qualify via regionals: Europe 2, Africa 2, Americas 1, Asia 3, plus auto 12 — the 12 auto plus 8 via regionals means Kenya can qualify via Africa 2 as 2-1 over Zimbabwe, not ranking alone — the 20's 12 auto is Super 8 plus host, not just ranking, which is why 2026 hosts India and Sri Lanka auto plus 2024 Super 8 eight plus 10 via regionals =20.

explainers.question: What is the Tour de France?
explainers.short: Tour de France, explained
explainers.answer: The Tour de France is cycling's 21-stage, 3-week Grand Tour over about 3,400km in July — 8 riders per team, 22 teams, yellow for the overall leader by time, green for sprint points, polka dot for mountain points, white for best young, with the winner decided by total time, not stage wins.
explain: The Tour is 21 stages over 23 days with two rest days, about 3,400km — 7 flat stages for sprinters at 50 km/h, 6 mountain stages in the Pyrenees and Alps with 2,000m climbs like Alpe d'Huez, 6 hilly medium, and 2 time trials where each rider races alone against the clock. The yellow jersey is the lowest total time — not most wins — so a rider who wins no stage can win the Tour if he is 2nd on every mountain, which happened in 1968.

The jerseys explain the parallel races. Yellow is overall time, green is sprint points at intermediate sprints and stage finishes, polka dot is mountain points at summits by category — hors catégorie highest — white is best under-26 by time, so one stage has four competitions: the break takes the polka, the sprinter takes green, the GC favourite protects yellow, the young rider attacks for white, all in the same 180km road.

The team explains the win. Twenty-two teams of 8 — 18 WorldTour plus 4 wildcard — ride as a train: domestiques fetch bottles, set tempo on the climb at 20 km/h to drop rivals, and the leader sits in the wheels at 30% less wind until the last 2km, so the Tour winner is the strongest who also has the strongest team — the leader's 7 helpers can be the difference between keeping yellow by 8 seconds or losing it on the Ventoux.

Time gaps decide more than stages. A flat stage win is often 0 seconds gap — the bunch finishes with the same time — while a mountain stage can create 2 minutes — the GC is won in the 3 mountain stages where gaps open, not the 7 flats where the bunch finishes together, which is why a sprinter can win 5 stages and be 100th overall, and a GC rider like Pogacar can win the Tour with 3 stage wins.

The evergreen myth is doping. The Tour's EPO era 1990s-2006 saw 7 Armstrong titles stripped, so the post-2010 Tour added the biological passport, where blood values are tracked longitudinally and a 2% reticulocyte swing triggers a target test — the 21-stage 3,400km is now the most tested event in sport, which is why the 2020-24 winners are seen as the clean generation, not the 2000s'.

Women's explains the gap. La Tour Femmes is 8 stages over 8 days in July after the men's, not 21 — the women's Yellow also by time, but over 950km, which started in 2022 after the old 14-stage version folded, so the men's Tour's 21-stage 3,400km remains the longest Grand Tour vs the Giro and Vuelta at 21 stages but about 3,200km.
explainers.example: July: Stage 17 to Courchevel — 165km, 5,000m climbing, break goes at km 10, polka leader takes 20 points on the Madeleine, Pogacar attacks on the last 7km at 20 km/h, gains 45 seconds on Vingegaard, yellow changes shoulders by 8 seconds, green sprinter finishes 25 minutes down but keeps green, 8 riders per team, 22 teams, yellow by total time, not the stage win.

myths.reality: 21 stages over 3 weeks — 7 flat, 6 mountain, 6 hilly, 2 time trials, 3,400km — yellow by total time, not most stage wins.

myths.belief: The yellow wins the most stages.
myths.reality: Yellow is lowest total time — a rider can win no stage and win the Tour if he is 2nd on every mountain, as in 1968.

myths.belief: Cycling is individual.
myths.reality: 8 per team — domestiques set tempo, fetch bottles, and shield the leader at 30% less wind until the last 2km, so the team wins the Tour.

explainers.question: How does golf actually work — and what are the four majors?
explainers.short: Golf majors, explained
explainers.answer: Golf is 18 holes, lowest strokes wins, with the four majors — Masters at Augusta in April, PGA Championship in May, US Open in June, The Open at links in July — each 156 players over 4 rounds of 18 holes, 72 holes total, cut after 36 holes to top 65 and ties, and the winner gets the green jacket, Wanamaker, or Claret Jug.
explain: The 18 holes explain par. Each hole has par 3, 4 or 5 — par 4 is 380-450 yards to the hole in 2 shots plus 2 putts, par 5 is 530+ with 3 shots, par 3 is 180-220 in 1 shot — the course par is 70-72 over 18 holes, so 4 rounds par is 280-288, and the winner is the lowest over 72 holes, not the most holes won, which is why a 65 in round 1 and a 75 in round 4 can still be 280 total.

The four majors are separate owners. The Masters is Augusta National's invitational 88-90 players based on past champions and world ranking, the PGA is the PGA of America's 156, the US Open is the USGA's 156 with qualifying, The Open is the R&A's 156 links — the majors share no tour, so a LIV player like Koepka can play the majors via the qualifiers but not the regular PGA Tour's FedEx events, which is why the majors are the only place LIV and PGA meet.

The cut explains the weekend. After 36 holes (two rounds) the field cuts to top 65 and ties — about half go home Friday night — so the weekend is 70-85 players over 36 holes, with the leader teeing last on Sunday at about 14:30 local. The cut at 4 over can keep a 3-time major winner in while a world number 5 on 5 over goes home, which is why the Thursday-Friday grind is survival, not just score.

Why links matters is wind. The Open at St Andrews or Royal Liverpool is links — firm, treeless, wind 15-25 mph — so the ball bounces 40 yards and pot bunkers trap, while the Masters at Augusta is parkland with soft greens that stop, so the same 7-iron is 150 yards at Augusta with spin and 130 at St Andrews with wind, which is why a Masters winner often misses the Open cut and the Open winner often misses the Masters cut.

The evergreen bottleneck is 72 holes. A 3-shot lead with 6 holes left is about 70% to win, but the 18th at Augusta or the 17th at Sawgrass can flip it — a double bogey 6 on a par 4 moves -10 to -8 and the chaser's 66 from -8 to -10 wins, which is why final-round 65s like Nick Faldo's 65 to win the 1996 Masters from 6 back are the myth that 6 back with 18 left is dead, not alive.

explainers.question: How do Formula 1 tyres work?
explainers.short: F1 tyres, explained
explainers.answer: F1 tyres are 5 dry compounds C1 hard to C5 soft plus intermediate and wet, with 2 dry mandatory per Grand Prix, pit window 1-2 stops, degradation 0.1s per lap vs 0.5s cliff, and the undercut vs overcut that 1 second pit vs 23s pit lane decides.
explain: F1 tyres are 18-inch Pirelli — 5 dry C1 hard (white) to C5 soft (red) plus C2-4 yellow, plus intermediate green and wet blue — each GP picks 3 dry of the 5: e.g. Bahrain C1-C2-C3, Monaco C3-C4-C5 — the 3 per GP plus 8 sets dry per weekend (soft 3 sets, medium 2, hard 1, plus sprint 2 extra?) — the tyre life is 25 laps soft, 35 medium, 45 hard on 2024's abrasiveness, so the degradation cliff at lap 12 for soft's 0.5s per lap after cliff vs 0.1s linear before decides the pit lap, not the fuel, which is why soft starter pits lap 18 while hard starter lap 30.

The 2-dry rule decides strategy. The Grand Prix must use 2 of the 3 dry compounds, so a soft start must finish medium or hard plus mandatory 1 pit — the 1 pit 23 seconds pit lane vs 0.1s per lap degradation makes the undercut vs overcut: pit lap 16 to undercut the leader's pit 17 with fresh medium 1 sec per lap faster — the undercut's 2s gap closes, which is why Verstappen at Monaco pits 16 from soft to hard to undercut Leclerc's 18, not stay out for overcut 20 with clear air but 0.5s degradation cliff.

The evergreen myth is soft always fastest. Soft is 0.8s per lap faster lap 1-5 but degrades 0.5s after cliff lap 12 vs medium's 0.2s after lap 25, so soft at lap 20 is slower than medium new — the soft's 25-lap life vs medium's 35 shows the crossover lap 18 where medium new beats soft old by 1.2s, which is why the 2-stop soft-medium-soft vs 1-stop medium-hard decides Monaco's 1-pit not 2 as tyre choice's crossover.

The pit lane 23 seconds plus stationary 2.1s vs 3.5s slow shows stop's window — the 23s at 60 km/h pit lane vs 350 km/h straight's gap 23s pit lane loses 23s plus 2.1s stop =25s total, so the undercut needs 0.8s per lap x 3 laps =2.4s to recover, which is why undercut lap 16 with 3-lap fresh delta recovers 2.4s vs leader's old soft degradation, not the 0.5 cliff alone — the 23s is the evergreen that makes 2-stop not 1 if tyre degradation's 0.5s after cliff times 10 laps =5s vs pit 25s, so 2-stop loses 50s vs 1-stop 25s but gains 1.5s per lap x 20 =30s, net 20s loss.

The sprint's one-tyre myth vs GP's 2. Sprint 100km uses one tyre no mandatory, GP 305km uses 2 mandatory, so sprint's soft 15 laps 30 minutes with no pit wins 0.5s per lap vs GP's soft-medium must 2 compounds — the 100km sprint's one tyre shows why sprint at Interlagos 24 laps soft only works but GP 71 laps not — soft life 25 not 71, so GP needs medium-hard 45.
explainers.example: Bahrain GP: 57 laps — 3 compounds soft C3 medium C2 hard C1 — Verstappen soft 18 laps then hard 39 laps 1-stop undercut Leclerc lap 17 medium, pit 23s +2.1s stop — soft 0.8 faster laps1-5 but medium new crossover lap18 beats soft old by 1.2s, so medium after cliff's 0.1 vs 0.5 decides — the 2-dry rule's soft-medium vs sprint's one-tyre no pit 100km with one soft not two.

myths.belief: Soft is always fastest.
myths.reality: Soft 0.8s faster laps1-5 but 0.5 cliff after 12 vs medium 0.1 — soft old at lap 20 slower than medium new crossover at 18 by 1.2s.

myths.belief: One tyre per race.
myths.reality: Grand Prix must use 2 of 3 dry — sprint 100km no mandatory, GP 305km 1-2 stops mandatory, so soft only not allowed at GP.

myths.belief: Pit is 2 seconds.
myths.reality: Stationary 2.1s plus pit lane 23s =25s — the undercut's 0.8×3=2.4s needs 3 laps fresh to recover 25s.

faq.q: How many tyre compounds in F1?
faq.a: 5 dry C1-C5 plus intermediate and wet — 3 per GP chosen (e.g. C1-3 Bahrain), 2 mandatory at GP.

faq.q: What is undercut?
faq.a: Pit 1 lap early with fresh tyre to pass — 0.8s per lap fresh recovers 25s pit lane in 3 laps.

faq.q: Does sprint need 2 compounds?
faq.a: No, sprint 100km one tyre no pit, GP 305km 2 compounds mandatory — soft only illegal at GP.

explainers.question: How does an F1 pit stop work?
explainers.short: F1 pit stop, explained
explainers.answer: An F1 pit stop is 2.0 seconds stationary plus 23 seconds pit lane — 3 gunners per wheel plus jack plus stabiliser 22 crew, wheel nuts single hex 400Nm, pit limiter 80 km/h, with 1-2 mandatory stops for 2 dry compounds, not 0 as sprint's one-tyre 100km, and the 2.0 vs 3.5 decides undercut vs overcut.
explain: Pit stop is 22 crew: 3 per wheel gunner plus off plus on =12, 2 jack front+rear, 2 stabiliser, 1 traffic light, 2 tyre carriers — wheel nut single hex captive 400Nm, gun 15,000 rpm with 0.8s on-off — the 2.0s stationary with 4 tyres is 4 guns simultaneous, not sequential, so Red Bull's 1.82s record at Brazil 2019 is 4 guns plus jacks in 1.82, not sequential 8s, which is why the 2.0 vs 3.5 decides the undercut's 0.8s fresh per lap recovers 25s pit lane not 2.0 vs 2.0 same, but slow crew 2.5 vs fast 2.0 is 0.5s extra — the 23s pit lane at 60/80 km/h plus 2.0 stationary =25s total, not 2.0 alone.

Pit lane speed 60 Monaco vs 80 elsewhere plus 23s at 60 vs 18s at 80 decides cheap SC 10s vs green 25 — pit lane open under SC/VSC vs closed if incident — the pit limiter 80 electronic vs pit 60 at Monaco with 23s vs 18s, so Monaco 18s not 23, which is why Monaco pit 18s total 20s vs Bahrain 23+2.1=25s 5s faster — the 1-pit Monaco 1st wins with 18s not 25, so Monaco's 1-pit strategy wins with 18s vs 2-pit 36s not 50s, which is why Monaco overtakes 0 + pit 18 decides race, not DRS's 15 mph with no zone as Monaco.

The 2-dry mandatory 1-2 stops decides — mandatory 2 compounds means 1 pit minimum with soft-medium, 2-pit medium-hard-soft for degradation 0.5s cliff at 12 — the pit window lap 16-30 decides undercut with 1 pit vs 2 pits — the sprint 100km uses one tyre no pit, GP 305km uses 1-2 pits for 2 compounds, so sprint's soft 15 laps 100km with no pit wins 0.5s per lap vs 2 compounds — the 2-dry rule's 1 pit minimum with soft-medium, 2-pit 2 stops 50s vs 1-pit 25s, but fresh tyre 1.5s per lap x 20 =30s net faster, which is why 2023 Bahrain Verstappen soft 18 hard 39 1-pit vs others 2-pit soft-medium-hard 2 pits 50s but gain 30s net loss 20s, so 1-pit wins at Bahrain with degradation 0.1 linear before cliff not 0.5 after.

The jack vs penalty explains 2.0 still. The traffic light green when all 4 guns off plus jacks down, red if wheel not on — penalty 5s if pit lane speeding plus 80 limiter's 0.2s per 1km/h over — the 2.0 stationary includes 0.3s reaction plus 1.7s guns — the 2.0 record 1.82 not 1.5 with 22 crew vs NASCAR's 5 crew 12s sequential? Actually NASCAR 5 lug sequential 12s vs F1 1 capture simultaneous 2.0 — the 1.82 vs 12 shows 22 vs 5 crew plus single nut vs 5 lug nuts, not skill alone.

The evergreen myth is pit stops decide race. Tyre compound C1-C5 choice plus SC 10s vs VSC 6s plus constructors 70% car plus DRS 15 decides more than pit lane 23s — the pit lane 23s is 23 of 90sec lap 25% lap time, which is why the pit lane 23s cost is 25% lap with pit entry plus 23 plus exit plus 2.1 =25s vs lap 90s, so undercut's 2 laps fresh 1.6s vs 25s not just pit 2.0, which is why the 2.0 stationary not pit lane decides Monaco's 18s vs Bahrain's 25s.
explainers.example: Red Bull Bahrain: 57 laps soft 18 hard 39 1-pit 2.1s +23s lane =25s vs 2-pit 50s but fresh 30s gain — front jack + rear jack + 3 per wheel 22 crew 4 guns simultaneous 1.82 record — pit limiter 80 60 Monaco 18s vs 23s — the 1-2 mandatory 2 dry compounds vs sprint 100km one tyre no pit — the undercut lap16 0.8×3=2.4s vs green 25s decide, not just stationary 2.0.

myths.belief: Pit is 2 seconds total.
myths.reality: Stationary 2.1s plus pit lane 23s =25s — Monaco 18s with 60 limit vs 23s at 80 — SC cheap 10s vs green 25.

myths.belief: One pit always.
myths.reality: 1-2 mandatory for 2 dry compounds — soft-medium 1 pit vs medium-hard-soft 2 pits 50s vs 25s with 30s fresh gain.

myths.belief: Crew is small.
myths.reality: 22 crew 3 per wheel plus jacks plus carriers — 1.82 record simultaneous 4 guns vs NASCAR 5 lug 12s sequential.

faq.a: Stationary 2.0s record 1.82 plus 23s pit lane =25s — 22 crew 4 guns simultaneous, 2 dry mandatory pit 1-2.

faq.q: What is pit lane limit?
faq.a: 80 km/h (60 Monaco) + limiter — 23s lane 80 vs 18s Monaco 60 — SC cheap 10s vs green 25.

faq.a: 1-2 for 2 dry compounds — sprint 100km one tyre no pit, GP 305km 2 compounds need 1 pit.

explainers.question: What are constructors vs drivers championships in F1?
explainers.short: Constructors vs Drivers, explained
explainers.answer: Drivers' is one driver's sum of 25-1 points over 24 GPs, constructors' is team's sum of both drivers' points over 24, with $1bn prize split 14-10% to top team, not the drivers' trophy, with Red Bull's 1st+2nd 25+18=43 per GP vs Williams 11th 1 point, so constructor shows car 70% not driver 30%.
explain: Constructors vs drivers: drivers' championship is driver's 24-race sum 25-1 to 10th plus fastest if top10 — Verstappen's 575 2023 with 19 wins vs Pérez 285 was drivers' 1 vs 2, constructors' is team's sum Verstappen 575 plus Pérez 285 =860 for Red Bull 1st vs Mercedes 2nd 409 (Hamilton 234+Russell 175) =860 vs 409, so Red Bull's constructors 860 not Verstappen alone 575 shows team 70% car plus 2-driver sum vs driver 30% individual — the constructors' 860 prize 14% $140m vs Williams 10th 28 points $15m with cost cap 135m shows car, not pay driver, wins constructors not drivers.

The prize split myth: drivers' trophy is Drivers' (Fangio) trophy with driver's name, constructors' Cup with team trophy $1bn split Pro Rata 14% for 1st (140m), 10% 2nd, 7% 3rd... not equal — the 14% not 5% shows team's $140m vs 9th's $35m with wind-tunnel handicap last 115% vs first 70% aero hours, not equal car, which is why Williams 10th with 28 points prize 35m plus merch 10 not 140 still needs $135m cap gap with owner subsidy vs Red Bull's 860 prize sufficient.

The grid's evergreen myth is drivers equal cars. Drivers not equal as car decides 70% pace — Red Bull's 1-2 43 per GP vs Haas 0 shows car not driver, which is why Pérez 2nd in same car vs Hamilton 3rd in Mercedes 2nd — the same car 1 vs 2 gap 290 points Verstappen-Pérez 290 not 0 shows driver 30% within team, but between teams car's 70% decides 860 vs 409 gap, not Hamilton's 234 beating Pérez's 285? Hamilton 3rd but Mercedes 2nd with Russell sum 409 shows team sum not driver best.

explainers.question: What is Formula 1 — and how does it work?
explainers.short: Formula 1, explained
explainers.answer: Formula 1 is 20 drivers in 10 teams in single-seaters at 220 mph over 24 Grands Prix per season from Bahrain in March to Abu Dhabi in December, with points 25-18-15-12-10-8-6-4-2-1 to 10th per race, the constructors' sum of both drivers, and DRS and budget cap as the modern bottlenecks.
explain: Formula 1 is 10 teams of 2 drivers — Red Bull, Mercedes, Ferrari, McLaren, Aston Martin, Alpine, Williams, RB, Sauber, Haas — each builds a 798kg hybrid single-seater with a 1.6L V6 turbo plus 120kW hybrid, at 220 mph on the straight, 5g in corners, with 18-inch Pirelli tyres in 5 compounds from soft to hard and intermediate and wet for rain, so the car, not just the driver, decides about 70% of pace by data.

Weekend explains the evergreen. Three practices Friday-Saturday, qualifying Saturday over Q1, Q2, Q3 knockout — 20, then 15, then 10 — with the fastest lap on soft taking pole, then the Grand Prix Sunday over 190 miles or 2 hours, 44-78 laps by track, with a formation lap, a standing start with 5 lights, and a pit window where the 2-second tyre change can undercut — the 24 weekends are the 24 tracks, from Monaco's 2-mile street to Spa's 4.3-mile mountain.

Points are 25 to 10th. Winner 25, 2nd 18, 3rd 15, 4th 12, 5th 10, 6th 8, 7th 6, 8th 4, 9th 2, 10th 1 plus fastest lap 1 if top 10, so a 1-2 team takes 43 and the 10th takes 1, and the constructors' championship is the sum of both drivers — Red Bull's 1st and 2nd in 2023 was 43 every Sunday, which is why the team title often follows the drivers' title.

DRS explains the overtake. The Drag Reduction System opens the rear wing on a straight if within 1 second of the car ahead at the detection point, adding about 15 mph and 20m of closing — the DRS zone is 600-800m, so the following car gains, not the leader, which is why the lead car defends by braking early to be within 1 second for the next DRS, and why Monaco has no DRS pass while Monza has 3 DRS zones.

The budget cap is the evergreen since 2021. Teams are capped at $135m per season for car development, not driver salaries, so wind-tunnel time is also capped by championship position — last gets 15% more wind tunnel than first — which is why the 10th in December gets more aero hours next year, not more money, and why the 2021-22 caps decided the 2023 pecking order more than the drivers did.

explainers.question: What is a Formula 1 sprint weekend?
explainers.short: F1 sprint, explained
explainers.answer: A sprint weekend is a Friday qualify + Saturday sprint + Sunday Grand Prix format over 6 weekends a year — the sprint is 100km (about 30 minutes) with points 8-7-6-5-4-3-2-1 to 8th, no pit stop needed, separate from the Grand Prix's 25-18-15 on Sunday, with sprint qualifying (SQ) setting the sprint grid.

Sprint points explain MYR. Sprint top 8 get 8-7-6-5-4-3-2-1, GP top 10 get 25-18-15-12-10-8-6-4-2-1 — sprint 8 for 1st is 32% of GP's 25 — the sprint's 8 vs 25 means a sprint win is not GP win, so Verstappen's 4 sprints 2023 with 4 wins 32 points — total 575 with sprints vs 543 without, which is why the sprint's 15-20 laps with no mandatory pit vs GP's 44-78 with 1-2 stops decides strategy: sprint full attack with one tyre, GP 2-stop managing lilac.

Qualifying split matters. SQ is Friday 15:12:15 with soft only, with SQ1 12 min 5 out, SQ2 10 min 5 out, SQ3 8 min top 10, medium? fact? The sprint's 2024 rules SQ has medium at SQ1 SQ2? Actually sprint SQ may mandate medium — the GP qualifying Saturday is normal soft-hard with Q1 Q2 Q3 18:15:12 with soft — the Friday SQ vs Saturday qualifying grid difference explains why some team qualifies 1st Sunday but 7th sprint, as Leclerc 2023 Baku did.

Tyr's sprint vs GP tyre. Sprint uses one tyre no mandatory stop — most start soft or medium and go to 100km with no pit, GP uses 2 compounds mandatory with pit window 1-2 stops — the sprint's 100km 30 minutes with 15-20 laps in street not pit, which is why sprint at Sprint? Actually Brazil's 100km 24 laps São Paulo 100km 24 laps 30 min with no 2-second pit, while GP 71 laps with 2 stops 1:30 race time 71 laps tyre split soft-medium-hard, not just sprint's one.

The evergreen myth is sprint is the race. Sprint is shorter than the 305km GP — GP 190-305km vs sprint 100km — sprint sets sprint points 8 not GP pole at GP. Since 2024 sprint pole not counted as GP pole — Verstappen 2023 had 7 sprint poles but 32 GP poles counted, not 39 — sprint pole is sprint not GP, which is why the sprint weekend's 2-pole weekend has GP pole for Sunday and SQ pole for Saturday, not the sprint pole for GP.

explainers.question: How does rugby league differ from union?
explainers.short: League vs union, explained
explainers.answer: Rugby league is 13-a-side, 80 minutes, 6 tackles then handover, no rucks, no lineouts, 4-point try plus 2 conversion plus 2 penalty and 1 drop goal, with NRL 17 teams and Super League 12, with State of Origin 3-game Queensland vs NSW, with league's 0-6 tackle count not union's ruck contest, with 10m onside not union's gate.
explain: League 13 vs union 15 is 2 fewer — league removes 2 flankers, so 6 forwards plus 7 backs =13 vs union 8 forwards plus 7 backs =15 — league 6 tackles then handover at 0-6 count, union ruck contest after tackle with release plus gate — league play-the-ball vs union ruck — the 6 tackles with 0-6 call by referee with 10m defensive line vs union's offside line hindmost foot — the league 6-tackle handover not union's ruck contest with tackler roll away plus gate plus jackal — league's 4-point try then 2 conversion plus 2 penalty plus 1 drop goal vs union 5 plus 2 plus 3 plus 3 — league 4 vs union 5 with 1 point gap plus conversion 2 both not 5 — the 4 vs 5 shows league's 8-0 vs union's 7-3 in NRL's 8 tries 32 vs union's 3 tries 21.

The NRL vs Super League myth: NRL 17 teams 24 rounds home-and-away plus magic Round plus finals 8 of 17 top 8 playoffs double elimination with 2 weeks finals then grand final vs Super League 12 teams 27 rounds 12 vs 12 home-and-away plus Magic plus 6 playoffs — State of Origin 3-game June-July Queensland Maroons vs NSW Blues 52,000 Suncorp with Origin 3-game with 40m kick return vs NRL 17's 35,000 average — league's Origin 3-game not union's 6 Nations 6-team 5-round 4 points plus bonus not 6-team 5 with try bonus — the 13 vs 15 with 6 tackles shows league's 0-6 then handover 6th tackle kick not union's ruck's 15 vs 15 with 80 minutes 2x40 both — the league's NRL grand final October at Accor 82,500 vs Super League grand final October at Old Trafford 60,000 with 13 vs 15 not 15's Twickenham 82,000.

explainers.question: How does rugby sevens actually work?
explainers.short: Rugby sevens, explained
explainers.answer: Rugby sevens is 7-a-side, 7 minutes per half (14 total), same pitch as 15s but 7 not 15, 5-point tries, no lineout? Actually lineout 2-man, scrum 3-man, with Olympic 12 teams over 3 days and World Series 8 stops — the fastest team sport where 14 minutes is the final, not 80.
explain: Sevens is 7 per side over 14 minutes — 2x7 with 2-minute halftime, 3 subs, sin bin 2 minutes not 10 — space is 7 of 15 on 100m so gaps 10m vs 2m in 15s, which is why the centre's speed 9m/s beats the lock's 7m/s — the sevens' try 5 points plus 2 conversion same as 15s, but conversions are drop-kick not place, and scrums are 3 not 8 with hooker 1 lock 1 prop, lineout is 2 not 8 with jumper 1 lifter 1, which is why sevens looks like sevens not 15-shrink.

The World Series explains season. The HSBC SVNS 2024 has 8 stops: Dubai, Cape Town, Perth, Vancouver, Los Angeles, Hong Kong, Singapore, Madrid final — 12 men's teams 12 women's, each stop 3 pools of 4, top 8 to quarters single KO — the Series winner is points per stop, not one final, which is why Argentina men 2023-24 won Series with 5 stop wins plus 2 finals, while NZ women 6 titles, not a single World Cup like 15s' 7 weeks, so the Series is the 8-stop 12 not the 20 of 15s World Cup.

Olympic 12 is smaller. explainers.question: How do sin bins and red cards work in rugby?
explainers.short: Rugby cards, explained
explainers.answer: Rugby cards are yellow 10 minutes (2 in sevens) with 14 men, red is 14 men rest of game but since 2024 the 20-minute red lets the team replace after 20, so the game returns to 15 vs 15 but the sent-off player is gone — the orange 20-minute vs permanent decides, not just yellow vs red as in football's red still 10 men.
explain: The yellow is 10 minutes in 15s (2 in sevens) with 14 men — tackled for cynical offside, high tackle at shoulder with no head contact mitigation, repeated team offside 3 penalties in 10 — the sin bin's 10 is 12.5% of 80, sevens 2 is 14% of 14 so proportional — the player returns after 10, so the 14 vs 15 is temporary, which is why the penalty try plus yellow for collapsing the maul is 5 points plus 10 minutes, not just 5, and why the 2023 law's bunker review for head contact tests yellow or red before the 10 or permanent, not after as football's VAR red straight.

The 20-minute red replaces the tackled red permanently. Since 2024 the orange 20-minute red: a red card for head contact with mitigation can be 20-minute sanction — the team is 14 for 20 then 15 again with replacement, but the player not returning — a deliberate foul or dangerous with no mitigation is full permanent red with 14 rest of game — the 20 vs full is bunker TMOs decision with 8-minute window, which is why France vs Wales 2024 had a 20-minute red not permanent, the player off but team back to 15 after 20.

The high tackle decision tree explains yellow vs red. Tackle height above shoulder plus head contact plus force plus mitigation (dipper, no time, no control) — high plus head with no mitigation is red or 20-minute, high plus shoulder with mitigation is yellow 10 — the tree's 3: yellow, 20-minute, permanent, which is why the 20-minute exists for mitigation not mitigation's yellow vs red binary — the head's risk vs shoulder's level plus dip's mitigation's 2 steps decide, not the foot as football's DOGSO.

The evergreen myth is red always 14 vs 15 to end. The 20-minute red returns to 15 vs 15 after 20, so the game is numbers-equal after 20 unless permanent — the 20's replacement is a non-offending bench player, not the sent-off, so the team's 23 becomes 22 plus 15, which is why the 2024 England vs Ireland's 20-minute red at 62 minutes left 14 until 82, then 15 for the last 10, not 14 for last 20, like 6 Nations' 1 yellow vs permanent's full.

The penalty try plus card explains double. A maul collapse to stop try is penalty try 7 points plus yellow 10 for the tackler — the 7 plus 10 double where football's DOGSO is red alone with no penalty goal's 7 — the rugby 7 plus 10 is the double where football's red is 1 zero plus 10 vs 11 for rest, which is why the maul's penalty try plus yellow is 7 plus 10, not just 7 as football's no-card penalty would be.

explainers.question: How does rugby union actually work?
explainers.short: Rugby union, explained
explainers.answer: Rugby union is 15-a-side, 80 minutes (2x40), where you carry not dribble, must pass backwards, tackle to the ground, and score 5 points for a try in the in-goal, 2 for the conversion kick, 3 for a penalty kick and 3 for a drop goal — the scrum and lineout are the set pieces that have no football equivalent.
explain: The backward pass explains the shape. Rugby is carried, not dribbled, and the ball must be passed backwards or flat, never forward — a forward pass is a scrum to the other team — so the team moves forward by running through the gain line, not by passing forward, which is why the 10-12-13 centres run the crash and the 9-10 pivot pass back to the wing.

The tackle explains the contest. A tackle brings the ball carrier to ground, the carrier must release, and both sides compete for the ball over it — the ruck — where the tackler must roll away and the arriving players must stay on their feet and enter through the gate behind the hindmost foot, so the breakdown is a second contest after the tackle, not a foul, and clean ball from the ruck lets the scrum-half pass.

The scrum is the restart for minor infringements. Eight forwards per side bind — 3 front row of loosehead, hooker, tighthead, 2 locks, 2 flankers, 1 number 8 — and the scrum-half feeds the ball mid-tunnel, the hooker hooks, and the pack pushes on the referee's crouch-bind-set, with penalties for early push or wheeling — the scrum is a shoving contest that can win a penalty 30 metres out, which is why South Africa pick 6 locks on the bench as the Bomb Squad.

The lineout is the throw. When the ball goes out, the hooker throws 5-15m between two lines of jumpers lifted by teammates, with the jumper who catches forming a maul — a driving bind — that can march 20m, so the lineout is the platform for the rolling maul try that looks illegal but is legal if the ball stays at the back and the maul does not collapse.

Scoring is 5+2+3+3. A try is 5 for grounding the ball in the 10-22m in-goal, conversion is 2 from the spot in line with the try 20m out, penalty 3 through the H posts, drop goal 3 on the run — a 5-point try plus 2 makes 7, so a 3-point kick is less than half a try, which is why teams chase tries at 14-12 down late, not kicks, and why the Six Nations table has 4 points for a win plus bonus for 4 tries or losing by 7.

Discipline is cards with teeth. A yellow is 10 minutes in the sin bin with 14 men, a red is 14 men for the rest after the 2023 law — and since 2023 a 20-minute red lets the player be replaced after 20, so the game is 15 vs 15 again but the sent-off player is gone — the 20-minute red is the bottleneck that changed 6 Nations discipline more than any law since.
explainers.example: Six Nations at Twickenham: England vs France, lineout 10m from the line, England jumper catches, 8-man maul forms, drives 12m, scrum-half passes to the 9 who dives for the try — 5 points, conversion from the touchline for 2 makes 7, France reply with a drop goal on 78 for 3 to make 7-3, England win with 7 vs 3 — the 5+2 vs 3 arithmetic that decides every rugby game.

myths.reality: Tackle to ground plus ruck plus backward pass — the ball must be released after the tackle and contested on feet through the gate, not dribbled or passed forward.

myths.belief: A try is 6 points.
myths.reality: 5, plus 2 for the conversion kick — 7 total, less than half for a penalty's 3, so tries are chased over kicks.

myths.belief: Scrums are just restarts.
myths.reality: A scrum is a pushing contest that wins penalties 30m out — South Africa's Bomb Squad of 6 locks wins games at the scrum alone.

explainers.question: How does the Rugby World Cup work?
explainers.short: Rugby World Cup, explained
explainers.answer: The Rugby World Cup is 20 nations every 4 years over 7 weeks — 20 play 4 pools of 5 over 4 weeks, top 2 to 8-team single knockout, winner plays 7 games, 48 games total, with 4 points for win plus bonus for 4 tries or losing by 7, not football's 3 points, with the 20th via repechage, not byes.

Points vs football explains bonus. Win 4, draw 2, plus 1 bonus for 4 tries or losing by 7 or less — bonus can flip 2-1 record's 9 points vs 3-0 on 12 but 1 with 4-try bonus — Scotland beat Tonga with 4 tries bonus 45-17, vs Samoa loss by 7 gets 1 losing bonus 12-14, which is why the 4 pools table's 1st on 15 can be 3 wins plus 3 try bonuses, not 4 wins like football's 9.

explainers.question: What is the Rugby Championship?
explainers.short: Rugby Championship, explained
explainers.answer: The Rugby Championship is the southern 4-nation July-September — New Zealand, South Africa, Australia and Argentina play home-and-away double round-robin 6 games each over 7 weeks, 12 games total, 4 points for win plus try and losing bonuses, not the Six Nations' single round where February cold not July sun decides.
explain: The Rugby Championship is 4 nations 6 games each — each plays the other 3 twice, home and away, 2 vs NZ at Eden Park, 2 vs SA at Ellis Park, 2 vs ARG at Vélez — 12 games total over 7 weeks with one bye per team — the Championship's 6 per team vs Six Nations' 5 per team is one more game, but the Championship's 2x home-and-away vs Six Nations' single 2H-3A alternate yearly — the 2x means the Ellis Park altitude 1,750m's advantage repeats for SA not just alternate, which is why NZ's Eden Park 30-year unbeaten home vs Six Nations' Twickenham 82k alternate matters differently.

Points as Six Nations: 4 for win plus bonus for 4 tries or losing by 7, so 6-game max 30 plus? Actually 6 wins =24 plus 6 try bonuses maybe 30, not 23 as Six Nations' 5-0 Slam bonus 3 — the Championship's 6-0 not 5-0 has no Slam bonus 3, so the 6-0 max is 24 plus 6 =30 with no extra, which is why NZ's 6-0 2023 with 5 try bonuses 29 beats SA 4-2 with 2 bonuses 18 by 11 not 3 as Slam would.

The evergreen is Argentina 2012. Argentina joined 2012 as 4th after Tri Nations 1996-2011 with 3 — the 4th made 6 from 4, not 4 from 3 — the Pumas' 2022 win over NZ at Christchurch and 2023 over Australia at Parra shows the 4th not dead weight — Wales' Six Nations Wooden Spoon 2023 with no wins vs Argentina's 2-4 still competitive, which is why the Championship's 4 closed not 6 as Six Nations with Italy, so Arg never Spoon but can be 4th with 0-6.

The myth is closed 4 forever. The Championship's closed 4 vs Six Nations' fixed 6 — no promotion as Europe's Rugby Championship plus Georgia vs 2023 6-0 Portugal repechage not — the Championship's 4 plus Japan invite talk for 5 has no promotion, like EuroLeague's 18 licences not open qualifier, so the Championship's 12 games vs Six Nations' 15 with similar TV dollars shows the 4's double round has 12 vs 15 with not open promotion.

The July-September sun vs February rain explains style. The Championship's July winter in NZ/SA is 10°C dry with hard pitches vs Six Nations February 5°C wet heavy — the hard not heavy favours running rugby with 6 tries per game vs forward wet with 3, which is why the final's 6-game double round's running shows where Six Nations' 5-game forward shows the autumn internations November cross-hemisphere to decide world 1, not just the hemisphere's table.

explainers.question: What is the Six Nations?
explainers.short: Six Nations, explained
explainers.answer: The Six Nations is rugby union's 6-team, 5-round league each February-March — England, France, Ireland, Wales, Scotland and Italy play each other once, 2 home 3 away alternating yearly, 4 points for a win, bonus for 4 tries or losing by 7, with the Grand Slam for 5 wins and the Wooden Spoon for 0.
explain: The Six Nations is 6 teams in a single round-robin — 5 games per nation over 7 weeks in February-March, with one bye week and one fallow week, so the championship has 15 games total, each 80 minutes, with no semi or final — the table after 5 decides, which is why the last Saturday has three games at 14:15, 16:45 and 20:00 to stagger the deciders, like football's last day but with 5, not 38.

Points are 4 for a win, 2 for a draw, 1 bonus for 4 tries, 1 bonus for losing by 7 or less — so a team can get 2 points from a loss with 4 tries and a close margin, and a 5-0 Grand Slam winner gets a 3-point bonus for the Slam, so 5 wins is 20 plus 3 = 23 max, while a 4-1 without bonuses is 16 — the bonus makes a 4-try win more valuable than a 3-try win even with the same 4 points for the win.

The venues alternate yearly. England at 82,000 Twickenham with 82,000 for France, France at 80,000 Stade de France, Ireland at 51,700 Aviva, Wales at 73,000 Principality, Scotland at 67,000 Murrayfield, Italy at 68,000 Olimpico — the 2-home-3-away flip each year decides the title as much as form, because a year with England away at France and Ireland is harder than the home year.

Why the Six Nations is not the Rugby Championship is the hemisphere. The Rugby Championship is 4 teams — New Zealand, South Africa, Australia, Argentina — in July-September with 2x home-and-away, so the Six Nations' February cold and rain produces forward-led low-scoring games, while the Championship's July sun produces running rugby — the same sport in opposite seasons, which is why the Six Nations winner and the Rugby Championship winner meet in the autumn internationals to decide the world number one.

The Wooden Spoon is the evergreen myth. No trophy, but the last-placed team is said to hold the Spoon — Italy have 18 since joining in 2000, Wales have 12, England 12 historically — and the Spoon in 2023 was Italy who beat Wales in Cardiff to avoid it, so the bottom game in round 5 can be as charged as the top, because the Spoon, like relegation, is the anti-title that still fills the stadium.
explainers.example: Last Saturday 2023: Ireland need a win at home vs England to win the Slam — 4 points plus 3-point Slam bonus, France need a bonus-point win and an Ireland loss to overtake, Wales vs Italy is Spoon decider in Rome — Ireland win 29-10 with 4 tries for the Slam and 13-point bonus, France win with bonus but stay on 19, so the Slam bonus decides the table by 3, not points difference alone.

myths.belief: The Six Nations is knockout.
myths.reality: Single round-robin 5 games per nation over 7 weeks, 4 points for a win plus try and losing bonuses, Grand Slam bonus for 5 wins, no semi or final.

myths.belief: Bonus points decide draws.
myths.reality: 4 tries gets 1 bonus win or lose, losing by 7 gets 1 — a 4-try loss beats a 3-try win on bonuses, which is why teams chase the 4th try at 30-10 even when the win is gone.

myths.belief: It is always the same venues.
myths.reality: 2 home 3 away alternating yearly — a year with France and Ireland away is harder than the home year, which decides many titles.

explainers.question: What is the United Rugby Championship?
explainers.short: URC, explained
explainers.answer: The United Rugby Championship is 16 club sides from 5 nations over 18 rounds — Ireland 4, South Africa 4, Wales 4, Scotland 2, Italy 2 play 18 games not home-and-away, with cross-conference 6 vs 12, then top 8 single KO quarters and final, not the 6 Nations' national single or the Premiership's single-country 10.
explain: The URC is 16 clubs from 5 nations — Leinster, Munster, Ulster, Connacht from Ireland; Bulls, Stormers, Sharks, Lions from South Africa; Scarlets, Ospreys, Cardiff, Dragons Wales; Edinburgh, Glasgow Scotland; Treviso, Zebre Italy — 16 play 18 rounds: 12 vs own shield? Actually 4 shields Irish, Welsh, South African, Scottish-Italian — each plays each shield rival home-and-away plus 12 cross, so South African 4 vs each other 6 not 6 cross — the cross is 6 vs 10 plus 2 extra, which is why Irish shields decide Champions Cup slots with 1 per shield plus next 4 on table, not table 1-8 alone like Premiership's 10.

18 rounds explains table. Eighteen rounds over 21 weeks September-May, then 8-team knockout quarters single at higher seed, semis at higher seed, final at highest remaining — the 18 not 22 as France's Top 14 26 nor 10-team Premiership 18 with home-and-away — the URC's 18 with shields 6 internal plus 12 cross vs Top 14's 13 home-and-away with 13 reverse, which is why URC's shield winner can be 5th overall but qualify for Champions Cup via shield 1, not table 9 like Welsh 4th shield 7th overall still qualifies.

Why Stormers explains the south. Since 2021 South African 4 joined from Super Rugby — Stormers Cape Town 18k, Bulls Pretoria 51k at Loftus, Sharks Durban at Kings Park, Lions Johannesburg at Ellis — the URC final 2022 Cape Town Stormers win over Bulls 18-13 was first south final at Cape Town, not Murrayfield — the 2024 Glasgow beat Bulls at Pretoria final — the south's 18k-51k crowds vs Cardiff's 8k shows the south's pull, like IP's 132k Ahmedabad vs domestic 20k.

Champions Cup gate matters. RGC shares Champions Cup slots: Irish shield 1 plus next 3 Irish on table plus each shield winner? Actually top 8 URC qualify for European Champions Cup plus Challenge Cup for next 8 — the 8 from 16 is half, so Leinster on table 1 not just shield, plus Bulls 2, Glasgow 4, Ospreys 8 as Welsh shield — the gate is 8 of 16 vs Premiership's top 8 of 10, which is why Ospreys 8th on 50 still qualifies while Connacht 9th on 49 needs Challenge, not Champions, and why Italian Treviso with 9th Shield Italian 1 can be out of 8 but Shield Italian 1 to Challenge, not Champions as next 4 would.

The evergreen myth is URC is European only. The 16 includes 4 South African from Super Rugby since 2021 — the cross-hemisphere not just European as Top 14's 14 plus Pro D2 16 — the URC's 18 rounds single KO vs Premiership's home-and-away 18 with 4-team playoff semi double plus final single — the cross vs south shows the league's 5-nation vs nation, which is why URC's final can be in Pretoria with 51k Loftus not Twickenham's 82k as national final, with south 4 of 16.
explainers.example: 2023-24 URC: Glasgow beat Bulls 21-16 final at Pretoria — 16 clubs 5 nations 18 rounds over 21 weeks — Irish 4, SA 4, Wales 4, Scotland 2, Italy 2 — Stormers win 2022 at Cape Town — 8-team KO quarters single at higher seed — 8 to Champions Cup via shields plus next 4, not just table 1-8 — the cross 6 internal shield plus 12 cross, not home-and-away double.

myths.reality: 16 clubs 5 nations — 4 Ireland, 4 SA, 4 Wales, 2 Scotland, 2 Italy 18 rounds — South African 4 since 2021 from Super Rugby.

myths.belief: URC is home-and-away double.
myths.reality: 18 rounds: shield internal plus 12 cross, not double all 15 — 7th overall can qualify as Welsh shield 1 not table 9.

myths.belief: URC final is Murrayfield.
myths.reality: Higher seed hosts — Glasgow at Pretoria 2024, Stormers at Cape Town 2022 with 51k Loftus, not neutral Twickenham 82k.

faq.a: 16 from 5 nations — 4 Ireland, 4 SA, 4 Wales, 2 Scotland, 2 Italy — 18 rounds then 8-team single KO.

faq.a: Regional shield: Irish, Welsh, SA, Scottish-Italian — shield winner qualifies for Champions Cup even if 7th overall.

explainers.question: How does swimming at the Olympics work?
explainers.short: Swimming, explained
explainers.answer: Olympic swimming is 35 events — 17 per gender plus 1 mixed medley relay — per stroke over 50m to 1500m in a 50m long-course pool, with heats, semis and a final where 0.01 decides, 0.00 is a touchpad, and the 8-lane final has no best-thirds — 16.00 makes the final, 16.01 goes home, which is why 0.01 is the evergreen margin.
explain: The pool explains the time. The long course is 50m, 8 lanes, 2.5m per lane, with touchpads that stop on 0.01 and a false start beep for the dive — the short course 25m is 2 seconds faster per 100m because of more turns and push-offs, so Olympic records are long course only, which is why the 100m free long course is 46.80 and short course 44.84 for the same swimmer — the turns, not the water, decide.

The strokes explain the 35. Freestyle 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1500, backstroke 100 and 200, breaststroke 100 and 200, butterfly 100 and 200, individual medley 200 and 400, plus relays 4x100 free, 4x200 free, 4x100 medley, plus the mixed 4x100 medley — the medley relay order is back, breast, fly, free so the back starts in the water, which is why the mixed medley's order can be man-woman-man-woman in any stroke but the back must start.

Rounds explain the week. The 100m has heats 64, semis 16, final 8 over two days — 64 in the morning heats, 16 in the evening semis, 8 in the next evening final — so a swimmer who makes the final swims 3 times, which is why the heats are at 80% to save the 0.01 for the final, and a 16th on 48.02 who ties for 16th swims off at 21:00 with one lane — the swim-off is the evergreen 0.01 decider that football has no equivalent for.

Why 0.01 is not photo is the pad. The touchpad is 2m by 1m at the end, pressed by the hand, not the head, at 0.01, so a finish with a fingertip vs a palm can be 0.02 — the pad, not the eye, decides, and the Omega quantum timer in 2024 resolved to 0.001 for the judges but displayed to 0.01, so a 0.001 tie is still 0.01 on the board and the swim-off decides, not the thousandth.

The suit explains the 2009-10 records. The polyurethane suit that covered the body added buoyancy and was banned in 2010, so the 2008-09 records in the suit still stand in some events — the 100m free suit record of 47.05 was beaten only in 2023 by 46.80, 15 years later, which is why the evergreen question is which records are suit-era and which are post-suit textile, and why the 1500m freestyle has not been broken since 2023.

Relays explain the team. The 4x100 free relay is 4x100 per nation, 8 nations in the final, with relay takeovers measured at 0.00 — the next swimmer can dive when the incoming touches, so a -0.10 takeover is a disqualification, which is why the relay's 0.00 exchange is the football offside line of swimming.
explainers.example: Paris 2024 final night: Men's 100m free final — 8 lanes, 46.80 winning, 2nd 47.04 by 0.24, women's 100m breast — 1:04.40, heats 1:06.00, semis 1:05.00, final 1:04.40 — one touch on the pad at 0.01 decides 16th vs 17th in the heats, and the 4x100 medley relay final has the backstroker start in the water at 0.00 takeover, no best-thirds, 0.01 on the pad is the final, not the table.

myths.reality: 35 events — 6 frees 50-1500, 4 strokes x2 distances, 2 medleys, 3 relays plus mixed medley — heats, semis, final where 0.01 on the pad, not points, decides.

myths.belief: Short course is the same.
myths.reality: 25m vs 50m — short course is 2 seconds faster per 100m because of more turns and push-offs, so Olympic records are long course only, 46.80 vs 44.84 for 100m free.

myths.belief: A tie can share gold.
myths.reality: If 0.01 ties, the tie is displayed as the same time but the judges' 0.001 may split it — a swim-off decides 16th vs 17th, and a final tie can share if 0.01 still ties.

faq.a: 25m has more turns and push-offs per 100m than 50m — about 2 seconds per 100m faster, so Olympic 50m records are long course only.

faq.q: What is a swim-off?
faq.a: A tied 16th on 0.01 swims again at 21:00 for the 16th final spot — the 0.01 tie-break that football has no equivalent for.

explainers.question: How does tennis seeding actually work?
explainers.short: Tennis seeding, explained
explainers.answer: Tennis seeding puts the 32 best ranked into 32 of 128 at a Slam by ranking, with the 1 vs 32, 2 vs 31 on opposite halves, so the 1 and 2 can only meet in the final, the 1 and 4 only in the semi, and unseeded vs seeded is the first-round upset, not by draw luck.
explain: Tennis seeding is 32 of 128 — the top 32 in ATP or WTA enter as seeds 1-32, 32 seeds in a 128 draw means 32 seeds vs 96 unseeded in round 1, with seeds staggered so 1 plays the winner of 128 vs 33 section, not 1 vs 2 up top — the 1 vs 32 path is 1 vs 32 in the fourth round if chalk holds, not in the first, which is why the 33rd ranked is the floater who can draw the 1 in round 1 while the 32nd cannot.

The draw halves matter. Seeds 1 and 2 are opposite halves — 1 top half, 2 bottom — seeds 1-4 are quarters, so 1 can only meet 2 in the final, 1 vs 3 or 4 in the semi, 1 vs 5-8 in the quarter, which is why the US Open semi can be 1 vs 4 and the final 1 vs 2 if 1 and 2 win 6 rounds each, and why the Wimbledon grass seed can bump the ranking seed for the grass one slot, not randomly.

The unseeded floater is the evergreen upset. The 34th ranked unseeded can draw the 1 in round 1 and win 3 of 10 — Botic van de Zandschulp vs Carlos Alcaraz at US Open 2024 was unseeded vs 3 seed on day 1, not day 7 — the 33-128 floaters fill the 96 holes, so the first-round seeded upset is floater vs seed, not seed vs seed, which is why the qualifier at 180 can meet the seed at 12 in round 1 while 12 vs 13 is saved for round 3.

The seeding vs ranking gap explains protection. The seed protects for 3 rounds — 1-8 get a pass to round 3 vs 25-32, 9-16 vs 17-24 is round 3 — so a protected 6 can lose in round 1 to a floater at 45 if the floater's 3 is hot that day, but the 6's path to the quarter is 32, 17-24, 9-16, 5-8 — the ladder holds if the seed wins, but the half's 96 floaters mean the ladder's upset is daily, not weekly like football's 38.

The myth is seeding is ranking. Wimbledon until 2021 used grass formula with 75% grass points, so Federer at 3 in 2019 was seeded 2 — the ATP ranking decided 32, the grass formula decided the 1-32 order — since 2022 it mirrors ranking, but the 1-2 halves still hold, which is why the Slam draw show's ball 1 and 2 are drawn to opposite halves live, not by computer alone.
explainers.example: US Open 2024 draw: 128 draw, 32 seeds — Sinner 1 vs Mackie 110 first round, Alcaraz 3 vs Li Tu 186 first round lost, seed 1 vs seed 32 is round 4 not round 1 — 1 and 2 opposite halves, so Sinner 1 path quarter vs Medvedev 5, semi vs Draper 25, final vs Fritz 12 — the 32-seed protection that still sees 3 of 32 lose day 1 to the 33-128 floaters, and 1 vs 2 only in the final.

myths.belief: Seeding is random.
myths.reality: 32 of 128 by ranking, 1 and 2 opposite halves, 1 vs 32 round 4 if chalk, so 1 can only meet 2 in the final, not round 1.

myths.belief: The best 32 get easy round 1.
myths.reality: They play 1 of 96 floaters 33-128 — the 34th can draw the 1 round 1 and win 3 of 10, so the floater is the upset, not seed vs seed.

myths.belief: Seeding equals ranking.
myths.reality: 32 by ranking but order can shift — Wimbledon grass formula until 2021 moved Federer 3 to 2 — now ranking mirrors but 1 and 2 halves still drawn live.

faq.q: How many seeds at a Slam?
faq.a: 32 of 128 — 1 and 2 opposite halves, 1 vs 32 round 4, 1 vs 2 only final, 96 floaters 33-128 draw seeds round 1.

faq.q: Can the 1 play the 2 early?
faq.a: No, 1 and 2 opposite halves, 1-4 quarters, so 1 vs 2 final only, 1 vs 3 or 4 semi.

faq.q: Who can draw the 1 in round 1?
faq.a: Any floater 33-128 — the 34th was van de Zandschulp vs Alcaraz 3 at US Open 2024, unseeded upset day 1.

explainers.question: How does a tennis tiebreak work?
explainers.short: Tennis tiebreak, explained
explainers.answer: A tiebreak is first to 7 by 2 at 6-6, with serve rotation 1-2-2-2, and the Slam final-set tiebreak since 2022 is first to 10 by 2 at 6-6 — the tiebreak replaces the endless deuce game at 6-6 to decide the set in about 20 minutes, not 60.
explain: The 7-point explains the set. At 6-6, the tiebreak is first to 7 by 2 — the server serves 1 point, then the returner serves 2, 2, 2 until 7 — so the serve pattern is 1-2-2-2, change ends after 6 points, which is why the 6-6 game can end 7-6(3) where the winner took 7 points and loser 3, and why the score is 7-6(7-3), not 7-3 — the tiebreak is the 13th game of the set, not the set's second half.

The 10-point is the Slam final difference. Since 2022 every Slam plays final set at 6-6 as first to 10 by 2, not endless — Australian, French, Wimbledon and US Open all 10-point final-set super tiebreak, so the 6-6 final is 10-8, not 16-14 as Isner-Mahut 70-68 was in 2010's endless fifth before the law — the 10 by 2 saves 30 minutes and the 70-68 will never return, which is why the final-set 6-6 is now 10-point, not advantage.

Why 6-6 matters is the break. Before 6-6 the set is 6 games by 2 — 6-4, 6-3 — with no tiebreak until 6-6, so a 5-4 lead still needs a break to 6-4 or tiebreak, which is why a 6-5 service game is break point not set point, and why the tiebreak's first-to-7 is about 20 minutes, not the 45-minute 8-6 that 7-6 replaces — the tiebreak's 7 vs 10 decides 10 sets per Slam more than the 6-6 would have.

The myth is tiebreak is first to 7 always. explainers.question: How does the ATP ranking actually work?
explainers.short: ATP ranking, explained
explainers.answer: The ATP ranking is a 52-week rolling points tally of a player's best 19 tournaments — 4 Slams plus 8 Masters 1000 mandatories plus 7 best other — with 2000 points for a Slam, 1000 for a Masters, 500 for a 500, 250 for a 250, and no points for losing first round — the ranking is the total, not the average.
explain: The 52-week roll explains movement. Points stay for 52 weeks then drop — a player who won the Australian Open for 2000 in January keeps them until next January, then defends them — so the ranking on Monday is last year's this week replaced, which is why Djokovic can be 1st without playing if his best 19 still totals more than Alcaraz's 19, and why a 3-month injury drops a player 30 places as 3 Masters worth 1000 each fall off with no replacement.

The 19 explain the ceiling. Four Slams (2000 each) plus eight Masters 1000 (1000 each) are mandatory if the player qualifies, so 12 of the 19 are fixed — the other 7 are best of the player's 500s, 250s, Challengers or United Cup — so a top 10 must play 12 plus about 7 more to keep 19, while a player ranked 80 plays 25 to find his best 7, which is why the top play 19 and the grinder plays 30 but the total is still best 19, not all.

Points per round show the ladder. Slam winner 2000, final 1200, semi 720, quarter 360, round of 16 180, round of 32 90, round of 64 45, round of 128 10 — so a quarter at a Slam is worth more than a 250 title (250), which is why a Slam quarter specialist can be top 20 without winning a title, and why a 250 title as a wild card is often the 19th that stays, not the top, for a top 10.

Why Masters are mandatory is the calendar. The 8 Masters — Indian Wells, Miami, Monte Carlo, Madrid, Rome, Canada, Cincinnati, Shanghai, Paris — are 96 or 56 draws, so 0 points for missing without medical exemption counts as a 0 in the 19, which is why a top player who skips Miami for rest takes a 0 that drags the total, not just a missed chance — the 0 is the evergreen myth that ranking is best 19, not 19 played, so a missed mandatory is a 0, not a free skip.

The live ranking vs the official explains Monday. The official ranking updates Monday after the Slam or Masters, but the live ranking during the tournament shows the points with last year's drop already removed — a player can be live 5th on Thursday and official 8th on Monday if the 2000 he defended last year was not re-earned this year, which is why the live moves during the event more than the official after.
explainers.example: Monday after the US Open: Sinner won 2000 for the US Open, kept his 2000 from last year's Australian that did not yet drop, dropped 360 from last year's Rome quarter that is now 52 weeks old, added 180 for this year's Rome round of 16 as his 19th — total 9,200, still 1st over Alcaraz on 8,500 who added a 1000 Miami win but lost a 2000 from last year's Wimbledon final that dropped that Monday — 19 best, 52-week roll, Monday update.

myths.belief: Ranking is all tournaments.
myths.reality: Best 19 — 4 Slams plus 8 Masters mandatories plus 7 best other — so 12 are fixed and 7 are best, not all 30 played.

myths.belief: Missing a Masters is free.
myths.reality: Masters are mandatory — a missed mandatory without medical is a 0 in the 19, not a skip, so it drags the total like a first-round loss.

myths.belief: Ranking is average.
myths.reality: Total of best 19 over 52 weeks — the 52-week roll means points drop after 52 weeks, so a 3-month injury drops 30 places as 3 Masters fall off.

faq.a: 2000 win, 1200 final, 720 semi, 360 quarter, 180 round of 16 — a Slam quarter beats a 250 title's 250.

faq.a: Best 19 — 4 Slams plus 8 Masters 1000 plus 7 best other over 52 weeks, dropping after 52 weeks.

faq.a: 0 points in the 19 if not medical — a mandatory 0, not a free skip, so the total drops.

explainers.question: How does the French Open work?
explainers.short: French Open, explained
explainers.answer: The French Open (Roland Garros) is the clay Grand Slam in late May-early June at Paris — 128 singles over 15 days on crushed brick 3mm, best of 5 men, 3 women, 10-point final-set tiebreak, no roof until 2020 on Philippe-Chatrier, with 5C heat of 25°C plus wind who makes the high 1.5m bounce at 24 km/h the topspin's 8-shot rally.
explain: The French Open is 128 at Roland Garros 15 days late May — 128 men, 128 women, 20 courts 1 roof since 2020 on Chatrier 15,225, best-of-5 men, 3 women, 10-point at 6-6 final set — the crushed brick 3mm over limestone with 60cm drainage makes the 1.5m high bounce at 24 km/h with 3,000 rpm topspin sitting shoulder-high, not knee — the high bounce plus 5C 25°C plus wind 15 km/h swirl in Chatrier open makes the 8-shot rally vs US Open hard's 5, which is why Nadal's 14 titles on Philippe-Chatrier's 60m2 vs SW19's 20m grass shows the surface + wind tank.

The seeding's clay specialist myth. Roland Garros has no extra grass formula — ranking seeds 32 as other Slams — the 32 seeds split halves, 1 vs 32 round 4, 1 vs 2 final, but the clay specialist at 15 can be floater 33 vs 1 in round 1 — the 15 clay specialist at 410 points before French can meet Sinner 1 in round 1 while 32nd at 310 cannot, which is why the French first-round seeded upset is clay floater vs seed, not hard specialist, and why the new night session on Chatrier at 21:00 with roof closed makes the 25°C open not the night closed's 20°C with no wind.

The evergreen is the night session. Since 2021 Roland Garros has one night match on Chatrier at 21:15 with roof available since 2020 — the 21:15 ticket is separate €300 vs day €120, which is why the day session 11:00 with 6 courts plus night 21:15 with 1 creates the 25°C open vs 20°C closed with Djoko night vs day advantage, like AO's night vs day heat but at 25°C not 35°C.

The mark vs Hawkeye explains line. Clay leaves a mark of 3mm, so Roland Garros used mark not Hawk-Eye until 2024 small courts Hawkeye — the umpire walks to the mark's 3mm, not the cam's 2.6mm, which is why RG's challenge is walk to mark, not 10-second graphic as hard's Hawkeye, and why the mark's wind can blur, so 2024 small Hawkeye replaces mark with 2.6mm cam same as hard.

The price explains the stadium. Roland Garros 2024 rebuild has 15,225 Chatrier with roof plus 10,000 Simonne-Mathieu plus 5,000 Lenglen — 1m attendance over 15 days vs SW19's 500k, SW19's queue vs RG's reservation — the crush 3mm vs hard acrylic 10mm drains 30mm/hour vs hard 0, so RG can play in 5mm rain with squeegee, not hard's cancellation, which is why RG's 15 days includes one Monday not Sunday as extra day vs AO's 14.

myths.belief: French Open is hard.
myths.reality: Crushed brick 3mm over limestone — 1.5m high bounce at 24 km/h, 8-shot rally vs 5 hard, 60cm drainage vs acrylic 10mm.

myths.belief: No night at RG.
myths.reality: Since 2021 one night match 21:15 on Chatrier with roof since 2020 — €300 separate vs day €120, 25°C open vs 20 closed.

myths.belief: Hawk-Eye at RG.
myths.reality: Mark 3mm until 2024 small-court Hawk-Eye — umpire walks to mark, not 10-second graphic, now 2.6mm on small courts too.

faq.q: When is French Open?
faq.a: Late May-early June Roland Garros — 128 over 15 days, crushed brick 3mm, 1.5m bounce at 24 km/h, 8-shot rally.

faq.q: Does RG have a roof?
faq.a: One since 2020 on Chatrier 15,225 — plus night session 21:15 since 2021, mark 3mm until 2024 small Hawk-Eye.

faq.q: How many titles did Nadal win at RG?
faq.a: 14 — the clay specialist's 3,000 rpm at shoulder vs 36 km/h grass knee, 14 days with mark vs Hawkeye.

explainers.question: What are the four Grand Slams in tennis?
explainers.short: Grand Slams, explained
explainers.answer: The four Grand Slams are the four majors — Australian Open (hard, Jan), Roland Garros (clay, May), Wimbledon (grass, July), US Open (hard, Aug) — each 128 players, best of 5 men, best of 3 women, 2000 ranking points to the winner, and the calendar Slam is winning all four in one year, last done by Rod Laver 1969 men and Steffi Graf 1988 women.
explain: The Slams are the majors because they are ITF not ATP — the ITF owns them, the ATP owns the Masters 1000, so the Slams have 128 players, 32 seeds, 64 first-round losers who still get $80k, and 2000 points vs 1000 for a Masters. The surfaces make the cycle: Melbourne hard is medium-fast, Paris clay is slow and high-bouncing, Wimbledon grass is fast and low, New York hard is fast with humidity — the same player must win on three surfaces in seven months to hold all four.

The season explains the order. Australian summer hard in January tests heat, Roland Garros clay in late May tests stamina with 5-hour rallies, Wimbledon grass two weeks later tests serve-and-volley transition on a surface that is green on Monday and brown by the semi, US hard in late August tests humidity and night matches under lights — the surface change is the evergreen reason a calendar Slam is rare, not just talent.

Best of 5 vs 3 decides the men's vs women's narrative. Men need 3 sets at Slams, women 2, so a men's 5-set can be 5 hours and a women's 2-0 can be 58 minutes — the Slams' best-of-5 for men is the only best-of-5 left after the Tour finals went best-of-3, which is why men's Slams produce comebacks from two sets down that women's cannot, and why the men's final is Sunday and the women's Saturday.

The calendar Slam vs career Slam myth matters. A calendar Slam is all four in one year — Laver 1969, Graf 1988 — a career Slam is one of each over a career — Djokovic, Nadal, Federer and Serena all have the career, not the calendar — and the Golden Slam is all four plus Olympic gold in one year, only Graf 1988, which is why the calendar remains the hardest evergreen, not the career.

The Australian heat rule shows the operation. Melbourne can suspend at 40°C heat stress, Roland Garros has a retractable roof on Philippe Chatrier since 2020, Wimbledon has a roof on Centre and No.1, US Open has two roofs — the Slams' roofs decide if the final finishes under lights at midnight, which happened at the US Open 2021 when rain pushed the women's semi to Arthur Ashe roof and the final to Sunday.
explainers.example: 2023: Djokovic won Australian hard, lost Roland Garros semi, won Wimbledon grass, lost US final — 3 of 4, not the calendar, while the women's 2023 was Sabalenka Australian, Swiatek Roland Garros, Vondrousova Wimbledon, Gauff US — four different winners, no calendar, which is why the Slams' 128-draw 2000-point four-surface cycle is the evergreen chase that 3 of 4 still feels like failure.

myths.belief: The Grand Slams are ATP events.
myths.reality: ITF majors with 128 players and 2000 points — ATP Masters are 56-96 players and 1000 points, so the Slams are the ITF's four, not the Tour's.

myths.belief: All Slams are on hard courts.
myths.reality: Australian and US are hard, Roland Garros clay, Wimbledon grass — three surfaces in seven months, which is why the calendar Slam is rare.

myths.belief: A career Slam is the same as a calendar.
myths.reality: Career is one of each over a career, calendar is all four in one year — only Laver men and Graf women have the calendar in the Open Era.

explainers.question: What is the Australian Open?
explainers.short: Australian Open, explained
explainers.answer: The Australian Open is the hard-court Grand Slam in mid-January in Melbourne — 128 singles over 14 days in 35°C heat, best of 5 men, 3 women, with tiebreak 10 at 6-6 final set, heat rule at 4.0 wet bulb, retractable roof on 3 courts, and the Slam where the hard's 30 km/h bounce plus 40°C heat makes the 5-hour semi 40°C court.
explain: The Australian Open is 128 at Melbourne Park 14 days mid-January — 128 men, 128 women, 16 courts 3 roofs (Rod Laver 14,964, Margaret Court 7,500, John Cain 10,500), best-of-5 men, 3 women, 10-point final-set tiebreak at 6-6 as all Slams since 2022 — the hard's acrylic 30 km/h bounce 1.2m at 20°C but 35°C air adds 2 km/h bounce speed and 10% ball fluff wear per hour, which is why 35°C Melbourne mid-January plays faster than Indian Wells 30°C March, and why the heat rule closes the roof at 4.0 wet bulb globe.

The heat rule explains the delay. The AO heat stress scale 1.0-5.0 with wet bulb 32.5°C — at 4.0 the roof closes and play stops 10 minutes to cool, at 5.0 suspension — 2023 had heat rule 3 days, 2014 had 4.0 closure for 3 hours, which is why the 35°C outside is 40°C court with no wind under roof vs SW19's grass 15°C rain roof, and why the night session at 22°C after 19:00 has 70% of ticket revenue vs day's 30% because day is 35°C risk.

The seeding's bottom half matters. The AO draw's 32 seeds as all Slams, live draw halves at Crown — the bottom half's night match at Rod Laver at 19:00 is prime, top half day at 14:00 heat — the 32 seeds split halves, 1 vs 32 round 4, 1 vs 2 final, which is why Djokovic's 10 AO titles came via bottom half 7 times with night matches at 22°C, not top half day heat, and why Sinner's 2024 AO came via top half day heat 35°C not night.

The Happy Slam myth is the crowd. The AO is the Happy Slam for player facilities — $500k appearance for qualifiers plus $105k round 1 — the Happy Slam's 1m attendance over 14 days vs Wimbledon's 500k, with ground pass $60 for outer — the 1m vs 500k attendance plus 35°C vs SW19's 15°C rain explains why the AO's 14 days January is now the richest with $86m prize vs Wimbledon's $65m, which is why the AO's court is hard 30 km/h with roof, not SW19's grass 36 with queue 8mm.

The evergreen is midnight. The AO night session can run to 02:00 with best-of-5 — Murray vs Kokkinakis 04:05 2023, Hewitt vs Baghdatis 04:34 2008 — the latest finish 04:05 with roof open wind 10 km/h under lights vs US Open's 02:26 latest — the 02:00 finish is the AO's hard plus heat's late vs Wimbledon's 21:00 curfew, which is why the AO's 35°C day plus 22°C night makes the 5-hour semi 22:00 still 30°C with roof closed.

myths.reality: Outdoor hard 30 km/h 1.2m bounce but 35°C air adds 2 km/h vs SW19 15°C — 3 roofs close at 4.0 heat, night session 22°C is the prime, not day heat.

myths.belief: It is not hot.
myths.reality: Wet bulb 4.0 closes roof — 2023 heat rule 3 days at 35°C outside 40°C court — midnight finishes 04:05 under lights, latest of Slams.

myths.reality: 1m attendance over 14 days vs Wimbledon 500k — $86m prize vs $65m, hard 30 vs grass 36 with ground pass $60 not £27 queue.
